# Block 1: One sample {.unnumbered} *Roughly 20 minutes. Part A is arithmetic you have done before. Part B is one question, and the rest of the session is its answer.* ## Part A: the question There is a jar of beans. What is the mean mass of a bean in it? You cannot weigh them all. In the session you weighed ten. That is the whole problem of statistics in one sentence: you want to know something about a population, and you can only afford to look at a sample. ### Your sample Set your seed. Replace both numbers with yours. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} student_id <- 12345678 # <- yours session_code <- 4271 # <- from the board set_my_seed(student_id, session_code) my_sample <- population |> slice_sample(n = 10) my_sample ``` ::: The book runs on the demonstration seed, so the ten beans printed below are not yours: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} demo_sample ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| bean_id| mass_g| |-------:|------:| | 1825| 0.659| | 191| 0.506| | 1466| 0.670| | 1261| 0.486| | 1278| 0.570| | 1042| 0.542| | 115| 0.503| | 655| 0.540| | 1088| 0.488| | 797| 0.519|
::: ::: ### The mean ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} mean(demo_sample$mass_g) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.5483 ``` ::: ::: Ask your neighbour what they got. It is different. Hold onto that. It is Block 2, and it is the only interesting thing that happens today. ## Part B: the standard deviation, the long way In the session you did this on paper. Here it is in code, in the same order, so that you can see the arithmetic rather than a black box. The SD asks: **how far is a typical bean from the mean bean?** You cannot simply average the distances, because they cancel. The positive and negative deviations sum to zero by construction, every time, for any data. So you square them first, average the squares, then take the square root to get back into grams. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} demo_sample |> mutate( deviation = mass_g - mean(mass_g), squared_deviation = deviation^2 ) |> summarise( n = n(), mean_g = mean(mass_g), sum_sq = sum(squared_deviation), variance = sum_sq / (n - 1), sd_g = sqrt(variance) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| n| mean_g| sum_sq| variance| sd_g| |--:|------:|---------:|---------:|---------:| | 10| 0.5483| 0.0398621| 0.0044291| 0.0665517|
::: ::: Check it against R's built-in: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} sd(demo_sample$mass_g) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.06655165 ``` ::: ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Do it with your own beans :::: ::::{.task-container} Run the longhand pipeline above on **your** sample, and confirm it matches `sd()`. Then answer this without running anything: if you deleted the `squared_deviation` line and used `mean(deviation)` instead, what number would you get, and why? :::: :::
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} my_sample |> mutate( deviation = mass_g - mean(mass_g), squared_deviation = deviation^2 ) |> summarise( n = n(), mean_g = mean(mass_g), sum_sq = sum(squared_deviation), variance = sum_sq / (n - 1), sd_g = sqrt(variance) ) sd(my_sample$mass_g) # the same ``` ::: `mean(deviation)` returns **zero**. Not approximately zero: exactly zero, up to floating-point representation. This is not a property of beans. It is a property of the mean. The mean is the point from which the deviations sum to zero, which is one reasonable way of defining what "the middle" means. So a measure of spread built on unsquared deviations from the mean is guaranteed to return zero for every dataset ever collected, which makes it useless. Squaring is one fix. Taking absolute values is another, and gives you the mean absolute deviation, which is a perfectly sensible statistic that history did not choose.
:::{.callout-note} ## Why `n - 1` and not `n`? Because you measured the deviations from *your* sample mean rather than from the true mean, which you do not know. Your sample mean sits, by construction, in the middle of your own data, so the deviations from it are slightly too small. Dividing by `n - 1` rather than `n` compensates. This is worth exactly the thirty seconds you have just given it. Do not let anyone detain you on it in week one. ::: ### What it looks like Ten beans is few enough to show every one, so show every one. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} demo_mean <- mean(demo_sample$mass_g) demo_sd <- sd(demo_sample$mass_g) ggplot(demo_sample, aes(x = mass_g, y = 0)) + geom_vline(xintercept = demo_mean, linewidth = 0.6) + geom_vline( xintercept = demo_mean + c(-1, 1) * demo_sd, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4 ) + geom_point( size = 3, alpha = 0.7, colour = colorspace::qualitative_hcl(1, palette = "Dark 3") ) + scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL) + labs(x = "Bean mass (g)", title = "One sample of ten") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Ten beans drawn from the jar. The solid line is the sample mean; the dashed lines sit one sample SD either side of it.](01-one-sample_files/figure-html/fig-sample-1.png){#fig-sample fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Part C: the question that matters Before you go on, commit to an answer. **Does the standard deviation get smaller if you weigh more beans?** **And the mean mass of a bean in the jar. Does that get smaller, larger, or stay the same as you weigh more beans?** :::{.callout-important} ## The SD does not shrink The SD is a fact about the beans. Some beans are big and some are small, and weighing more of them does not make them more alike. If you weighed all 2000, the SD would settle down onto a stable number and stay there. Say that out loud, because in the next chapter something appears that **does** shrink, and the contrast between the two is the entire point of this session. ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Convince yourself :::: ::::{.task-container} 1. Change your sample size from 10 to 100 and re-run. Does the SD get systematically smaller? Try it several times, with different seeds, before you answer. 2. `population` is the whole jar, which in real life you would never have. Compute the true SD: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} sd(population$mass_g) ``` ::: How close was your estimate from ten beans? Now do the same with 100. Something is improving here. If it is not the SD itself, what is it? 3. What is `mean(my_sample$mass_g) - mu`? :::: :::
**1.** No. The SD bounces around the true value of roughly 0.083 g and shows no tendency to fall. Try it: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} map_dbl(1:10, \(i) sd(sample(population$mass_g, 10))) map_dbl(1:10, \(i) sd(sample(population$mass_g, 100))) ``` ::: Both sets of numbers sit around the same value. The second set is *less variable*, which is a different claim and matters in Block 2. **2.** What improves is the **precision of your estimate of the SD**, not the SD. With ten beans your estimate wobbles; with a hundred it wobbles less. The quantity being estimated never moved. This distinction, between a thing and your estimate of the thing, is the one the whole session turns on. **3.** That number is your **error**: how wrong you are. You can only compute it because this is a teaching jar. Sit with the fact that in your dissertation you will not be able to, and that every technique in the rest of this module exists because of that.
:::{.callout-note} ## The recurring question, planted **Your replicate is a bean.** If you weighed the same bean ten times, how many beans would you have? Do not answer at length. Just notice the question. It comes back in every session of this module, and in session 8 it acquires a name and a body count. :::
